source.title: Variability of the Structural Coloration in Two Butterfly Species with Different Prezygotic Mating Strategies
source.abstract: Structural coloration variability was investigated in two Blue butterfly species that are common in Hungary. The males of Polyommatus icarus (Common Blue) and Plebejus argus (Silver-studded Blue) use their blue wing coloration for conspecific recognition. Despite living in the same type of habitat, these two species display differences in prezygotic mating strategy: the males of P . icarus are patrolling, while P . argus males have sedentary behavior. Therefore, the species-specific photonic nanoarchitecture, which is the source of the structural coloration, may have been subjected to different evolutionary effects. Despite the increasing interest in photonic nanoarchitectures of biological origin, there is a lack of studies focused on the biological variability of structural coloration that examine a statistically relevant number of individuals from the same species. To investigate possible structural color variation within the same species in populations separated by large geographical distances, climatic differences, or applied experimental conditions, one has to be able to compare these variations to the normal biological variability within a single population. The structural coloration of the four wings of 25 male individuals (100 samples for each species) was measured and compared using different light-collecting setups: perpendicular and with an integrating sphere. source.results: Results Wing coloration and reflectance spectra Polyommatus icarus and Plebejus argus males have similar structural blue coloration—as observed by the naked human eye—on the dorsal surface of their wings, as shown in the photographs in Fig 1A and 1B . This blue color is generated by the so-called ‘pepper-pot’ type photonic nanoarchitecture [ 32 ], which is typical for polyommatine Blues [ 11 ]. The reflectance data on the dorsal side of all four wings of the 25 male individuals measured using the integrating sphere setup were averaged by species. The curves were normalized to the main reflectance peaks in the blue to facilitate comparison. Fig 2 shows the characteristic reflectance spectra of the two species: both species have a distinct peak at approximately 400 nm in addition to characteristic color differences. There is a small (~15 nm) difference between the wavelength of the averaged maxima in the blue, and compared to P . icarus , the averaged spectrum of P . argus males has an additional shoulder at 320 nm, showing that the wing coloration is species-specific. These results indicate that the measurements performed with the standard normal probe may be affected by a larger error margin if single measurements are compared than the measurements performed with an integrating sphere. source.discussion: Discussion Measuring iridescent wings Structural colors, in contrast to colors generated by pigments, usually exhibit a certain degree of iridescence, which requires the color measurement to account for effects that may arise from changes in the angle of incidence of the incoming light on the reflecting surface [ 33 ]. The individual scales producing the coloration of butterfly wings have typical dimensions in the range of 100 μm ( Fig 10 ). Each of these scales is produced individually by a different cell during an only partially understood process of self-assembly [ 34 ]. Individual structural variations of few tens of nanometers cannot be excluded. These variations are sufficient to shift the color of the photonic nanoarchitecture because the size of the characteristic building elements in the case of Lycaenid butterflies is less than 100 nm [ 10 ]. As a consequence, even the wings of the same butterfly may exhibit some differences in color, even when measured with an integrating sphere, as shown in Fig 4 . Therefore, when rigorous comparisons are to be made, for example, between populations of the same species living in different geographic locations or for butterflies subjected to experiments in the laboratory, which may modify their coloration, measurements on a statistically relevant number of individuals are recommended. data.title: 蓝蝶翅膀上的纳米结构差异
data.brief: 两种同域蓝蝶雄性翅膀的结构色存在可测量的种间差异，但其个体内与个体间的变异提示，比较不同种群前需先摸清单一群体内的正常波动范围。

sections.title: 从一枚翅膀说起
paragraphs: 在匈牙利常见的两种蓝蝶——多眼灰蝶（Polyommatus icarus）与银斑蓝灰蝶（Plebejus argus）——雄性翅膀背面都呈现相似的蓝色。肉眼看去，二者几乎难以区分。但这片蓝色并非来自色素，而是来自翅膀鳞片上一种被称为“胡椒罐”型的光子纳米结构。
这种结构在灰蝶科中具有代表性。当光线落在鳞片上，纳米尺度的构造会与特定波长的光发生干涉，反射出蓝色。由于结构本身由细胞逐个装配而成，装配过程只被部分理解，因此即便是同一只蝴蝶的不同翅膀，颜色也可能存在细微差别。

sections.title: 统计上可分辨的种间差异
paragraphs: 研究者测量了每种各25只雄性个体、每只四片翅膀，共100个样本。使用积分球装置采集背面反射光谱后，按物种平均并归一化到蓝色主峰以便比较。
结果显示，两个物种的光谱在蓝色主峰附近存在约15纳米的波长差。此外，银斑蓝灰蝶的平均光谱在约320纳米处多出一个肩峰，而多眼灰蝶没有。这说明翅膀颜色具有物种特异性。
在近紫外波段，两种蝴蝶也表现出可被多眼灰蝶感知的显著差异。论文指出，雄性正是利用翅膀的蓝色进行同种识别。

sections.title: 角度带来的测量难题
paragraphs: 结构色通常伴随一定程度的虹彩——颜色会随观察角度变化。光谱角度测量证实，两种蝴蝶的鳞片都具有虹彩性。这意味着，若用标准垂直探头做单次测量并直接比较，误差范围可能比积分球测量更大。
积分球可以收集更宽角度范围的光，降低角度变化带来的干扰。论文在比较两种测量方式后指出，尽管垂直入射测量的变异范围更大、偏离平均值更多，但当对100组数据取平均后，物种间的差异仍然可分辨。
这一方法学细节对后续研究很重要：要比较不同地理种群、不同气候条件或实验处理下的结构色变化，首先需要知道单一群体内部的正常生物变异有多大。

sections.title: 个体内的微小波动
paragraphs: 论文提到，产生颜色的单个鳞片尺寸约在100微米量级。每个鳞片由不同细胞独立生成，期间的自组装过程尚未被完全理解。个别结构出现几十纳米的变异并不能排除。
对于灰蝶而言，光子结构中的特征构建单元尺寸小于100纳米。几十纳米的变动足以使颜色发生偏移。因此，即使使用积分球测量，同一只蝴蝶的不同翅膀也可能呈现颜色差异。
论文未给出这种个体内差异的具体分布范围，但明确指出它是进行严格比较时必须考虑的变量。

sections.title: 与标本收藏和观察的关联
paragraphs: 这项研究提示，若要用标本或活体观察来比较不同来源的蓝蝶结构色，单次测量或单只个体并不足够。论文建议，在进行种群间或实验条件下的严格比较时，应对统计学上足够数量的个体进行测量。
对于收藏中的干标本，论文未讨论干燥、老化或保存条件对光子纳米结构的影响，因此无法据此给出收藏建议。待核。
可以确定的是，同一物种内部本身就存在结构色变异。在将任何差异归因于地理或环境因素之前，先建立本地群体的变异基线，是这项研究传递出的方法学态度。

sections.title: 种间识别之外的线索
paragraphs: 两种蓝蝶生活在相同类型的栖息地中，但求偶策略不同：多眼灰蝶雄性采取巡逻式飞行，银斑蓝灰蝶雄性则偏 sedentary（定栖）行为。论文在摘要中提出，这种前合子交配策略的差异，可能使作为结构色来源的物种特异性光子纳米结构受到不同的进化影响。
不过，论文并未进一步给出这两种策略如何具体塑造了光谱差异的结论。约15纳米的主峰位移和320纳米处的肩峰，是当前数据能支持的物种特异性证据。
结构色在这里不仅是视觉现象，也是可测量的物理性状。它把生态行为、纳米结构与光谱数据放在同一框架下，而框架中的许多环节仍有待后续研究填充。
